text.p: A group critical of Procter & Gamble Co's olestra said Wednesday some people have gone to hospital emergency rooms with severe digestive symptoms after eating Pringles potato chips made with the fat substitute.

The consumer products giant, which also makes Tide laundry detergent and Crest toothpaste, reiterated it believes olestra is safe and said a "vast majority" of test market consumers have not reported problems to P&G's tollfree olestra hotline.
"For the small percentage of people who do, these are common digestive effects like you get from eating baked beans or broccoli or a bran muffin," a P&G scientist said.
None suffered permanent harm, the group said.
P&G has sold or given as samples over one-half million cans of Fat Free Pringles in Columbus, P&G's Allgood said. Only about 350 people called P&G to report concerns, he said.
About a dozen additional snack food companies have signed contracts with P&G to purchase olestra, whose brand name is Olean, he said. He declined to name the companies.
PepsiCo Inc's Frito-Lay Inc since April has test marketed potato chips and tortilla chips made with olestra.
"We're just not seeing that (adverse) type of reaction," Frito-Lay spokeswoman Lynn Markey told Reuters. "Consumers are telling us they like snacks made with Olean."

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved olestra for use in some snack foods. The FDA requires such products to be labeled, "Olestra may cause abdominal cramping and loose stools. Olestra inhibits the absorption of some vitamins and other nutrients. Vitamins A, D, E and K have been added."

An FDA spokeswoman said P&G files periodic reports about consumers who have called its olestra tollfree hotline. "To date, adverse event reports do not indicate to us any cause to change current conditions of approval or indicate olestra is unsafe under the current approval conditions," she said.
Those who went to hospitals may have had the flu, P&G senior scientist Greg Allgood said in a telephone interview.
Olestra, introduced a year ago, is made from soybean and cottonseed oils. It adds no fat or calories so foods with it have less fat and calories than those with traditional fats.
P&G is test marketing Fat Free Pringles in Columbus, Ohio.

The nonprofit Center for Science in the Public Interest, a health advocacy group, said in a statement prepared for a news conference in Columbus that 187 people called its own hotline about intestinal ills after eating the chips. Several went to hospitals with severe abdominal cramps and diarrhea, it said.
